accepted.name: online_revenue
accepted.description: The money on this line if it went through sales channel 2, otherwise zero. Summed over an article it is that article's channel-2 revenue; paired with offline_revenue it recovers the channel mix of its sales, which the plain sum of price destroys.
accepted.why_it_matters: item-sales is a sum of price; channel 2 is 71.7% of rows but the split is per-article, and an article selling only through one channel responds differently to the next week's demand than one selling through both

accepted.name: offline_revenue
accepted.description: The money on this line if it went through sales channel 1, otherwise zero. The complement of online_revenue; the two sum back to price exactly.
accepted.why_it_matters: channel 1 is the minority channel (28.3%) and articles concentrated in it are a distinct merchandising population; a brute-force price/sales_channel_id ratio does not isolate it

accepted.name: price_point_ending
accepted.description: The sub-unit (cents) part of the recovered retail price. price is the true price divided by 590 -- its quantiles times 590 land on 0.10, 9.99, 14.99, 19.99 and 299.00 -- so this isolates the price-point ending: ~0.99 for the standard retail ladder, ~0.00 for round prices (entry lines and high-ticket round figures).
accepted.why_it_matters: the same article is transacted at different prices as it is discounted, and the ending digit is the only within-row signal of where on the price ladder a line sits; it is non-monotone in price, so no pairwise ratio reproduces it

accepted.name: off_ladder_revenue
accepted.description: Revenue booked at a price that is NOT on the standard .9x ladder -- round-number prices, which in this catalogue are the entry-price lines and the high-ticket round figures. Zero on ordinary .99 lines.
accepted.why_it_matters: aggregated over an article this is the money-weighted share of its revenue coming from off-ladder pricing -- a markdown/promotion proxy, and markdown state is the main thing that moves next-week unit volume

accepted.name: catalogue_metadata_gaps
accepted.description: How many of the article's four sentinel-bearing attribute codes are the -1 unknown marker. Counts product_type (121 rows), graphical_appearance (52), colour_group (28) and perceived_colour_master (685); perceived_colour_value is excluded because it is -1 on exactly the same 28 rows as colour_group and would double-count. Expect 0 on ~99.2% of rows.
accepted.why_it_matters: one scalar for how incompletely an article is catalogued -- thinly-described SKUs are fringe, short-lived, low-volume lines; it also collapses four -1 sentinels that any numeric encoder would otherwise read as a magnitude

accepted.name: plain_dark_staple
accepted.description: The wardrobe-basic archetype: solid (unpatterned) surface AND dark perceived tone. Code 1010016 is Solid and tone code 4 is Dark, both identified by matching per-value counts against the quantiles. Solid is 47% of the catalogue and Dark 40.5%, so expect this on roughly 15-30% of articles.
accepted.why_it_matters: black/plain basics are the high-volume, low-seasonality end of a fashion catalogue; neither column alone says 'staple', and subtracting or dividing these two nominal codes is meaningless

accepted.name: plain_childrenswear
accepted.description: A solid-pattern article in the Baby/Children division. index_group_no == 4 is Baby/Children (34,711 articles): that code assignment is the one that reproduces the column mean 3.1715 and all three quartiles. Baby/Children is 32.9% of the catalogue and Solid 47%, so expect ~10-20%.
accepted.why_it_matters: plain kidswear is the multipack, replenishment end of the range -- high unit volume at low unit price, so its revenue profile differs sharply from both patterned kidswear and plain adultwear

accepted.name: marketing_engagement_flags
accepted.description: How many of the two set-or-missing account flags are set, 0 to 2. Both columns hold only 1.0 or null, so all their information is in their null-ness; the == 1 test reads null as 0, which is the correct reading. FN is set on 34.8% of accounts and Active on 33.9%, so expect a mean near 0.7 with all three levels populated.
accepted.why_it_matters: aggregated over an article's buyers this says whether its demand comes from marketing-reachable, campaign-responsive accounts or from walk-in traffic; a brute-force FN - Active or FN / Active is all-null garbage because NaN propagates

accepted.name: young_engaged_shopper
accepted.description: A shopper in the youngest quartile of the customer base (p25 of age is 24) who is also opted in to fashion-news marketing. Age nulls (1.16%) fall to 0, as does an unset FN. Expect roughly 8-13% of accounts.
accepted.why_it_matters: the trend-responsive cohort; an article whose buyers are concentrated here sells on campaign and novelty rather than replenishment, which changes how its past sales extrapolate to next week
